summary:
Ebonyi State stands under Nigeria's national framework. The source inventory contains no Ebonyi-specific statute, prosecution, arrest, court ruling, incident or state institution bearing on transgender visitors, so the national assessment applies here in full.

Ebonyi is not among the states that have adopted Sharia criminal law. The death-penalty provisions that operate in the twelve northern states which have done so do not apply within Ebonyi, and a trans visitor's exposure in the state is the federal Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 and its enforcement by the Nigeria Police Force, as documented at national level.
tangentialFactors:
Ebonyi's non-adoption of Sharia criminal law is the only fact in the inventory that distinguishes its legal position from other Nigerian states. The distinction is narrow: it removes capital exposure, not criminal liability, and the federal statute applies in Ebonyi as it does elsewhere in the country.

The absence of Ebonyi-specific reporting is not evidence of a lower enforcement rate. Documented enforcement in Nigeria is concentrated in the largest cities and in the northern states, and a south-eastern state of Ebonyi's size would be expected to generate fewer reported cases even at an identical underlying rate. The inventory carries no per-capita or state-level enforcement data, so no comparison between Ebonyi and other states can be made.
localsOnly:
No Ebonyi-specific information on state health services, custodial placement, state-level protection machinery or state anti-discrimination provision appears in the source inventory.

Residents of Ebonyi are not subject to the Sharia penal codes that prescribe the death penalty for same-sex conduct in twelve northern states. The federal statute and its penalties are the operative law in the state.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Ebonyi State Police Command has arrested, charged or prosecuted anyone under the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 is not sourced. No Ebonyi prosecution, conviction or custodial-placement record appears in the inventory.

The national sources state their own limits. The English Wikipedia page on LGBT rights in Nigeria contains no Ebonyi-specific statute or incident, and Human Rights Watch's 2016 report on the Act names no Ebonyi case. Whether that reflects no enforcement, no reporting, or both is unresolved.

No Ebonyi-level proposal or enactment on cross-dressing, public morality or gender presentation is sourced.
